title: Advice to 'find common ground/shared interests'
description: This latent fires on imperative-style advice-list items that instruct the reader to identify or leverage shared interests, hobbies, experiences, or values (often as a bolded heading like 'Find common ground:') typically as a strategy for starting conversations, connecting with people, or bonding socially. It activates most strongly on the canonical phrasing 'Find common ground'/'Find shared interests' followed by elaboration about using that commonality as a conversation starter or connection point, and more weakly on related advice about exploring neighborhoods, joining groups, or searching for local resources that share the same listicle/imperative format. It does not activate on general relationship or communication advice that lacks this specific 'shared interest/experience as connector' framing, such as instructions to listen actively, validate emotions, prepare arguments, or set boundaries, even though these appear in similar bullet-list advice contexts.

title: Suggested activities in advice lists
description: This latent fires on list items or suggestions within advice-giving text, especially bullet-point recommendations for bonding, self-care, or social activities (cooking together, tutoring, joining groups, creative hobbies) and on the empathetic framing/validation statements that often accompany such advice (e.g., 'It's admirable that...', 'You were reasonable...'). It activates on short, imperative or nominalized phrases that propose a concrete action item, often bolded as a heading, as well as on brief validating or judgment statements about someone's situation in advice-column style text. It does not activate on narrative description, factual explanation, or analytical reasoning that isn't part of an actionable suggestion or interpersonal validation—e.g., plain statements of events or technical content without an advice/suggestion or supportive-judgment framing would not trigger it.

title: Personal life-domain framing
description: This latent fires on phrases and short clauses that frame or categorize aspects of an individual's personal life—relationships, career, health, hobbies, daily routines—often in list-like, parenthetical, or question form. It activates on sentences that name or enumerate life domains (e.g., 'career, relationships, health'), pose reflective questions about personal habits or goals ('How much time do you have for your runs?'), or make evaluative statements about interpersonal dynamics (pressure in relationships, emotional manipulation). It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative sentences lacking this personal/self-reflective framing, nor on abstract statements unconnected to an individual's life circumstances or choices. The common thread is a structural or topical orientation toward categorizing or querying personal well-being and relational life, rather than any single fixed subject.

title: Interpersonal advice-giving in emotional/relationship contexts
description: This latent fires on sentences from an advice-giving persona addressing personal, emotional, or interpersonal dilemmas—validating feelings, recommending communication strategies, suggesting compromises, or gently reframing blame/responsibility. It activates on phrases like 'focus on your own feelings and needs,' 'your feelings are valid,' suggestions to consult a professional, proposed scripts for difficult conversations, and rhetorical questions posed to guide the advice-seeker toward self-reflection or a decision. It also captures refusals or disclaimers framed as caring boundaries ('I can't provide advice on...', 'I cannot provide a response that may be harmful'), since these share the same supportive-counselor register. It would not activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative statements lacking this therapeutic/advisory tone, such as descriptions of rules of a game, policy definitions, or neutral third-person reporting without any relational or emotional guidance component.

title: Interpersonal advice-giving suggestions
description: This latent fires on advice-column style text that proposes concrete relational or practical actions someone should take to resolve interpersonal conflicts or improve a situation—e.g., 'have a conversation with X,' 'ask a neutral third party to mediate,' 'consider compromising,' 'offer to help.' It activates strongly on imperative or suggestive sentences (often bolded headers like 'Offer to assist,' 'Bring a small gift,' 'Consider counseling') that recommend communication, mediation, boundary-setting, or self-care strategies in personal/social contexts (family, roommates, coworkers, partners). It does not activate on purely factual, descriptive, or narrative statements lacking an advisory or suggestive framing, nor on abstract argumentation without an actionable interpersonal recommendation (e.g., general statements about societal issues or definitions).

title: Conversational verdict-giving in advice responses
description: This latent fires on the interactional scaffolding of advice-column or interpersonal-judgment responses: rhetorical questions posed to the reader ('Can we agree to disagree?', 'Would you like that?'), direct verdicts or judgments ('the answer is no', 'NTA', 'I'd say no'), and hedged evaluative statements that weigh both sides before delivering a stance ('while I understand your concerns... you're partially in the wrong'). It activates on short, discourse-management phrases that frame or punctuate a judgment—transitions like 'So,', direct address to 'you', and closing rhetorical or clarifying questions—rather than on the substantive content of the advice itself. It would not activate on purely descriptive, narrative, or factual sentences that lack this second-person evaluative or dialogic framing, such as plain statements of events or technical explanations without an implied judgment or audience address.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often the following period or bold-markdown asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '2.', '3.', or '4. **'. It activates specifically on the token representing the list index itself, regardless of what topic or content follows in that list item, and appears across many different contexts (advice lists, step-by-step guides, ranked suggestions, reasons, etc.). It does not activate on the prose content of list items, on introductory sentences that merely precede a list ('Here are some suggestions:'), or on numbers used in non-list contexts like dates, quantities, or statistics; the trigger is the structural marker denoting sequence/order in an enumerated list.

title: Supportive relationship advice
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice-giving text (often in an interpersonal, relational, or emotional-support register) that validate the reader's feelings, offer reassurance, suggest a course of action, or frame a personal/social situation in terms of needs, boundaries, and mutual understanding. It activates on generic advice-column or counseling-style statements—e.g., 'you're not obligated to sacrifice your own well-being,' 'this might be worth addressing,' 'they can offer support and help you develop a plan'—that use a warm, second-person or empathetic tone to guide someone through a relationship, conflict, or personal-growth decision. It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative statements lacking this advisory/empathetic stance, nor on sentences that merely describe events without offering guidance, validation, or relational framing (e.g., plain descriptions, headers, or single words with no advisory content, though a few such fragments appear as noise).

title: Interpersonal advice-giving in relational conflicts
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/therapy-style text that address someone directly ('you') about personal relationships, emotions, or interpersonal conflicts—validating feelings, suggesting concrete relational actions (advocate, communicate, gather feedback, set boundaries), or asking reflective questions meant to guide the person through a relational or emotional situation. It activates on second-person framing of relationship dynamics (family, partners, coworkers, friends), affirmations of reasonableness/compassion, step-like recommendations for handling conflict, and open-ended coaching questions ('What's most important to you?'). It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or third-person narrative content lacking direct interpersonal address or advisory/validating framing, such as neutral descriptions of events or instructions unrelated to personal relationships or emotional support.

title: Retrospective alternative-action framing in advice text
description: This latent fires on advice-style discourse that frames what someone could or should have done differently, especially the transitional phrases that introduce a bulleted list of alternatives (e.g., 'A more thoughtful approach might have been to:', 'They could have:', '1. **') as well as closely related validating statements that reassure someone their actual action was reasonable ('You simply asked him to...') or reframe blame ('He should have been more supportive'). It activates on sentences performing the discourse function of hindsight evaluation, suggestion-introduction, or moral/behavioral judgment within advice-giving or interpersonal-conflict commentary (e.g., Reddit-style relationship advice, AITA-type responses), including numbered-list markers and short encouraging asides ('Don't beat yourself up', 'Be kind to yourself'). It does not activate on plain factual, descriptive, or narrative sentences that lack this evaluative/advisory stance or list-introducing structure, even if they discuss similar relationship or conflict topics without judging past actions or proposing alternatives.

title: Supportive self-help advice tone
description: This latent fires on encouraging, advice-giving language typical of self-help or coaching text: affirming statements ('That's great to have someone like that in your corner!'), validating remarks about growth and effort, and prescriptive tips for communication, listening, or personal improvement (e.g., 'use reflective listening', 'read widely', 'seek professional help'). It activates on short, upbeat, second-person or imperative phrasing that reassures the reader or offers a constructive step, often including bolded advice headers or bullet-style tips. It also picks up on fragments/list markers ('End', 'Pre', 'Take small') that appear within such advice-list structures. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, narrative descriptions without advisory or affirming tone, or technical/analytical content lacking the warm, encouraging, self-improvement register.

title: Empathetic validation opener in advice responses
description: This latent fires on the stock introductory or framing phrases used in advice-giving/therapeutic-style responses (e.g., Reddit-style relationship or personal advice) that validate, normalize, or empathize with the person's feelings or situation before elaborating, such as 'It's understandable that...', 'That's totally okay', 'You're not the only one who feels this way', or naming a relatable dilemma with a wry label like 'The age-old conundrum of...'. It activates on short, formulaic reassurance/validation statements and on whimsical naming of a common interpersonal predicament, typically at the start of a response segment. It does not activate on purely factual, argumentative, or narrative sentences that lack this validating or dilemma-naming framing, nor on detailed advice content itself once the empathetic setup is complete.

title: Relationship/self-help advice generalizations
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice-style text (often relationship, personal-development, or lifestyle coaching content) that offer generalized guidance, observations, or reflective framing about behavior, communication, and interpersonal dynamics -- e.g., 'model positive behavior,' 'this way, you'll ensure...,' or rhetorical questions probing motivations or patterns. It activates on soft, hedged, advisory or reflective statements that name a strategy or benefit ('reduce stress,' 'set a good example,' 'focus on shared interests') and on questions structured to help someone introspect about relationships, habits, or intentions. It is not simply about the topic of relationships or self-help, but about the advisory/reflective rhetorical move itself -- restating a principle, weighing pros/cons, or posing a guiding question -- so it would not fire on purely factual, narrative, or descriptive sentences lacking this coaching or reflective framing, even if they discuss similar emotional or relational subject matter.

title: Empathetic perspective-taking in interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on second-person statements that place the speaker imaginatively in the addressee's position ('in your shoes') or otherwise validate/assess the addressee's actions and circumstances, typically in an advice-column or interpersonal-judgment context (e.g., AITA-style responses, relationship advice). It activates on phrases expressing empathy or moral evaluation directed at 'you'—affirming that the speaker would have acted similarly, or noting what the addressee did or is owed/responsible for. It would not activate on general third-person narration, factual statements, or advice that lacks this direct second-person empathetic/evaluative framing, even if the topic (e.g., cooking, family conflict) is similar.

title: Interpersonal advice-giving language
description: This latent fires on sentences that give supportive, advice-column-style guidance about interpersonal or emotional situations, typically recommending communication, boundary-setting, validation of feelings, or concrete relational action steps. It activates on second-person or imperative statements that affirm the reader's feelings/rights ('you deserve...', 'your feelings are valid') or prescribe interpersonal strategies ('have an open and honest conversation', 'communicate your boundaries', 'seek feedback'). It does not activate on purely factual, narrative, or technical statements lacking this advisory/validating register, nor on advice about non-interpersonal tasks (e.g., pure how-to instructions with no emotional or relational framing) even if phrased imperatively.
